COVID: Education [5675]

By: Carol Albertyn Christie | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

Further information:
There has been so much uncertainty to deal with during our lockdown; infection rates are soaring , economies are crumbling and unemployement is rife. There is a great sense of anxiety with the uncertainty.

Professor Jonathan Jansen’s SABC interview where he suggested that we should just scrap the 2020 academic year has really upset the apple cart amongst educationalists and parents.

https://citizen.co.za/parenty/2270703/watch-prof-jansen-says-scrap-entire-2020-school-year-pass-all-students/

https://mybroadband.co.za/news/government/347959-scrap-school-year-and-pass-all-learners-professor-jansen.html

The Department of Education has said that his comments were irresponsible and premature.
Elijah Mhlanga, the spokesperson states that after lockdown the learners will only have missed half of a term. And that the Department of Education is working on a plan.

https://www.msn.com/en-za/news/other/dbe-dismisses-call-to-scrap-school-year-as-irresponsible/ar-BB12M1r1

There is no plan as yet. Understandably we haven’t seen the full force of Covid in our country yet.

All schools were closed on the 18th of March 2020.
Minister Angie Motshekga said at the time that “we have determined that schools should resume on 14 April 2020; unless determined differently. If that happens,we will communicate with parents. We are going to lose 10 school days as a result of the school closures.
To compensate for lost days, the June holidays will be cut short by a week. Once opened, schools will be encouraged to extend tuition hours.”
It was anticipated that pupils would return to school on the 14th of April, until Pres Ramaphosa extended lockdown for another two weeks.
He has also suggested that there may be a phased return for the citizens of South Africa.
What is the plan now and what does that mean for the learners of the country?
There is a pressure to get our economy back to work but the threat of Covid may not have passed.
While there is uncertainty, can we really afford to scrap a year as Jonathan Jansen suggests.
Carte Blanche sets out to see what the impact of the lockdown has been on education and what solutions there may be.
We have identified 4 schools to speak to in KZN, a private school, a rural school, a model C school and a township school. We have an academic at UKZN and have asked for an interview with the spokesperson of the Department of Education.
The questions that have been raised due to the Covid lockdown are;
- Are all the schools teaching at the moment?
- Private schools and model C schools seem to be teaching again on learning platforms. But what about the State Schools?
- What support has been given to schools?
- Can we make up the time that has been lost?
- Can our teachers cope with the new way of teaching via e learning and other platforms?
- When will it be safe to send the kids back to school?
- Its not just their education at stake but their health?
- How can we assure the protection of the pupils at schools where there is no running water and sanitation?
- Can we afford to have the class sizes that we had in the past – what about social distancing?
- What about fees? Should parents continue to pay if they are not receiving the teaching that they were promised and the childrena re staying at home?
- Will the divide between the haves and have nots just be increased at this time? Private schools have resources to technology and poorer schools don’t even have accessibility to data.
- Some of the children have also been negatively affected because they have not had access to te daily meal that the school provides.
- Parents are hungry and unemployed getting food is more important than education.
- There are solutions that have been suggested. Working on Saturdays, reducing the work load for the year. Shortening the holidays.
- Unusual times calls for unusual measures.
- Dr Imran Keeka says that 80% of our learners do not have the necessary facilities.
- There will be a huge amount of infrastructure to mobilise to get this working. Jojo Tanks and toilets. Connectivity.
- How will we cope if there is a 2nd and 3rd wave of COVID 19?
- And what about the psychological implication. Children will be unsettled. They will have experienced a great change in the world. Close ones may have died. How will they cope going back to school? Is there the necessary psychological support?
- Matrics?


Agreed to be interviewed.

1. Principal Swazi Shabangu - Susan Ngcobo Amaoti Inanda
0838253534
Nothing happening. No direction from department.
Not teaching. Trying to reach out to parents way forward academic year.
Parents aren’t working and more worried about food.
At school they used to provide free lunch.NGO provide food parcels.
They used to cook at school. Tried to get approval to feed at school but denied.

2.Clifton School Private Boys. All teachers teaching on microsoft teams. Mr Shaun McCabe 0848500860
will talk to us. Everything back to normal. Boys having lessons with teachers on line. They do sometimes struggle with connectivity. But with resources all going well.

3. Dr Sihle Memela. Principal of High Flats. Rural School. 120km away from Durban. 082 7648618
No education doesn’t know what is happening.
Sending some info on whatsapp.
Some people doing it and some people not.
Not sure if they will go back to teaching as they may not be getting raise in July.
Talk of turning school in boarding school.
Want all kids and teachers to be tested for Covid before they go back.

4. Prof Labby Ramrathan UKZN School of Education Studies 0826749829
15 Edgcot Rd Westville
Can make time up. Teach them not all content but skills they need to master.
Can work holidays and can work saturdays.
Not the end of the school year. Curriculum not so extensive.Doesnt agree with Jansen.

What is possible
Focus on elements competance progress into next grade
Essential elements of next grade
Subject specialist overall perspecive of curriculum

What element current curriculum

Distilled version of year. Most knowledge is worthwhile right now.

Content manage next year

Learner manager platforms

Poor infrastructure

Provide community members help

Can’t have 60 – 80 in class room

Open up spaces. Extend school hours

Opportunity avaliable

Reduce holidays difficult 1 week holiday, reduce, can also utilise Saturdays


5. Christine Mitchell - IT Teacher at Penzance Primary School Durban. 0833576105
Found software called SeeSaw. American software, for free during COVID for next two moths.
90% of kids are able to connect.
Can connect on phone.

6. Simon Moore - PMB Headmaster 0825570800
Video of School Teaching Bloopers
Humorous not detracting from serious from situation
Team work and unity.
Humanity prevailing.
Gave up part of holidays to prepare. Use microsoft teams. Zoom calls. Teachers upscaling themselves.
Teachers learning things.
On line registration that use comments very positive
Privileged in mid may
Head Girl Ntando Dube
Incredible work
Londiwe Mkhulise - Zulu Teacher

Waiting to hear from Spokes person DBE Elijah Mhlanga.

Covid Education


V/O
This is Imbali township in Pietermaritzburg, KZN, it’s where Nelson Mandela in gave his last public speech in 1961.

Friends Asanda, Ntando and Sphe live a couple of houses away from each other in the same road in Imbali , they have been friends their whole lives.

Ntando
“We’ve known each other since we were little children, we played on the roads.”

Sphe
“We played ball and we ran around and played the three tins game.”

Asanda
“Ja, the bond has lasted for us for the entire time, we have never really been separated, even though we go to different schools.”

V/O
For these 3 matric students, the COVID 19 pandemic has altered their futures forever.

V/O
According to UNESCO over 1.5 billion learners world wide are unable to go to school. Like South Africa, 191 countries have temporarily closed their educational institutions in an attempt to contain the spread of the COVID-19 Pandemic.

Asanda
“It has affected me like in a very negative way , cause we are stuck at home and we are not studying and time is not going to stop and wait for us. It is moving.

V/O
Ntando Dube won a scholarship to attend St Johns DSG a private school in Pietermaritzburg and is their current headgirl.

Ntando
“A lot of people in South Africa, especially my community did not understand the entire concept of the lockdown, because when it was delivered to us it was in English, so for the first period of lockdown people were roaming the street and unaware of what was going on.”







V/O
And for many in the townships, school was not just a place of education.

Link
The Covid 19 pandemic is first and foremost a health crisis but when the lockdown was announced and schools were closed millions of South Africa learners across the country lost the only daily meal they received at school.

V/O
Swazi Shabangu is principal of a primary school in Inanda. She has around 700 pupils in her care who relied on food from the school.

Claire
“Is any learning or teaching happening during this lockdown?”

Swazi
“Ah Claire I don’t want to lie to you, unfortunately nothing, most of children are hungry, all they have in mind is food.”

V/O
She could not ignore the plight of her starving learners and reached out to the Glenwood community in Durban who arranged relief food parcels, some of these went to child headed households.

Basil
“There are concernes about the curriculum, there are concerns about whether we can actually teach enough but then there are also real social concerns. What about my family, what about my children, what about me?

V/O
When the Covid pandemic developed educators certainly never anticipated the way it would unfold.
Basil Manuel is the executive director of NAPTOSA, the National Professional Teachers' Organisation of South Africa.

Claire
“Do you think this lock down has exposed the inequalities in our education system?”

Basil
“Absolutely, we forget that schools are all microcosms of society and they are different. So it is incorrect to assume everybody ended at the same place so some may have even started with deficvits before the lockdown came but certainly what the lockdown did do is exaggerate our very very vast differences.






V/O
Ntando acknowledges that she is in a priviledged position.

Ntando
“The lockdown hasn’t affected me much other than having to stay home and doing my schooling at home.So when I think about other people, the way in which the lockdown has affected me, isnt really major because I can still resume my life as normal as possible, where you have got friends of mine like Asanda and Sphe who arent going to school or getting any materials through their schooling.”

Claire Link
“eLearning is set to be the way forward for education during this period of lockdown and even though some learners do have access to this virtual learning, the vast majority of children in this country do not have access to the internet.”

V/O
Fundokuhle Secondary School is just down the road from where the friends live. Sphe and Asanda attended high school here.

Asanda
‘We need money to get the notes printed and we need the money for data to log into the links that they gave us, since it is lockdown we are suffering financially so getting money to print papers can also be a problem, so its not easy for us at all.”

V/O
Asanda and Sphe have no computers, no printers and struggle to connect to teachers.

Sphe
“Lock down has affected me. When I don’t understand things I need a teacher to help me.”

Christine
“I do feel that most of the concepts that we are teaching long distance will need to be taught again in a classroom setting purely for the fact that purely because some children are going to need the extra benefit or help from the teacher.”

V/O
Christine Marshall from Penzance Primary School is in charge of their on line platform and is reaching 80% of the learners. Parents are having to play a larger role in their children’s education.

Christine
“As a teacher and a mother we have found the situation very difficult, I am not going to sugar coat it at all, it is very hard working full time and still having two children at home to look after.”


V/O
NAPTOSA believes that on line teaching is only reaching 30% of all of South African learners. Which means that 10 million children have no contact at all. That is why other educators have said we have lost too much time and we should scrap this academic year entirely.

Prof Labby Ramrathan at UKZN’s School of Education does not agree.

Labby
My view is that there is a lot of noise in the curriculum and what we need to do and what we need to do is get through the noise and find what is meaningful in the curriculum and for me its looking at the competance to progress into the next grade.”

V/O
Simon Moore is the Principal of St John’s DSG , here school continues as usual but with the help of technology.

Simon
“We’ve only really lost two days I suppose at the end of term in March, when the lockdown was imminent and the schools had to close and from the 15th we have been teaching on line so the girls have not missed any real lessons time except for those two days so we are pretty much on track.”

V/O
Similarily Clifton School in Durban is ensuring that all of their boys are up to speed. Shaun McCabe is Head of the Arts.

Shaun
“As an independent school we are fortunate that the school has been able to provide , partiucularily boys on bursaries and scholarships, with an ipad and reliable data bundle and that has been extended to staff as well. But I am fully confident that matric students at most independent schools will be in a position to write their preliminaries and write their finals at the end of this year.”

Link
The Department of basic Education is confident that the 2020 year is still not lost and they have a comphrehensive recovery plan.

V/O
Some of the suggested plans include a staggered return back to school, loosing some of the July holidays and scrapping June exams.

Labby
“Catch up time should be a new norm now. We have 5 days of schooling there is no reason we can’t go to 6 days of schooling. We have school from 8 – 2:30 or therabouts there is no reason why we cant have a full day of schooling. So we need to think out of the box.”

V/O
More pressing for parents is whether the health of their children will be compromised if they return to school.

Claire
What are you worried about your learners. Do you think we can make up for time lost?

Swazi
“We are worried but its education versus life of people you know even the president needs to make that decision because you can’t say lets go back to school because we are worried when we known that Covid 19 is real.”

Sphe
“I am worried when I go back to school there will be too many of us in one classroom.”

Basil
“We know that at or schools in their present make up social distancing is almost impossible, but what I want to reassure people about is that no teacher union is going to sit back and certainly not NAAPTOSA and just say for the gettinb the year sarted lets just go back , no parent is going to do that and we are dealing with concerns about teachers saying you know I am 64, we are dealing with prents who are saying I am so terrified can I keep my child at home, these are real concerns. How many of our teachers in our schools are immune defficient. This is what we have put on the table with the DBE, with this I want to show how much thinking is going into this.”

V/O
There are no definite answers, we will have to see how the pandemic progresses but in the interim there many futures at stake.

Asanda
“When we were kids I usually spoke a lot about being a scientistst but then life has its ways you don’t always get what you want.”

Ntando
“And so it hurts to know that we grew up as children with the same aspirations to finish school go work, help out our families but there is a possibility that only one person out of the three will realise their dreams and it is heart breaking.”


Promo 1
Its affected 1.5 billion learners from 191 countries around the world, how is the COVID 19 pandemic lockdown affecting children’s education in South Africa.

Promo 2
Experts have said that we have lost to much time due to the Covid 19 lockdown and should just scrap the 2020 educational year. Should we just pass all the children or can we still salvage their education?

Promo 3
The Department of Basic Education is confident that the 2020 SCHOOL year is not lost (and they have a comphrehensive recovery plan.)

But can the 10 million learners who are not receiving
tuition at the moment catch up?

Prof Labby Ramrathan at UKZN’s School of Education does not agree. Labby My view is that there is a lot of noise in the curriculum and what we need to do and what we need to do is get through the noise and find what is meaningful in the curriculum and for me its looking at the competance to progress into the next grade.” V/O Simon Moore is the Principal of St John’s DSG , here school continues as usual but with the help of technology. Simon “We’ve only really lost two days I suppose at the end of term in March, when the lockdown was imminent and the schools had to close and from the 15th we have been teaching on line so the girls have not missed any real lessons time except for those two days so we are pretty much on track.” V/O Similarily Clifton School in Durban is ensuring that all of their boys are up to speed. Shaun McCabe is Head of the Arts. Shaun “As an independent school we are fortunate that the school has been able to provide , partiucularily boys on bursaries and scholarships, with an ipad and reliable data bundle and that has been extended to staff as well. But I am fully confident that matric students at most independent schools will be in a position to write their preliminaries and write their finals at the end of this year.” Link The Department of basic Education is confident that the 2020 year is still not lost and they have a comphrehensive recovery plan. V/O Some of the suggested plans include a staggered return back to school, loosing some of the July holidays and scrapping June exams. Labby “Catch up time should be a new norm now. We have 5 days of schooling there is no reason we can’t go to 6 days of schooling. We have school from 8 – 2:30 or therabouts there is no reason why we cant have a full day of schooling. So we need to think out of the box.” V/O More pressing for parents is whether the health of their children will be compromised if they return to school. Claire What are you worried about your learners. Do you think we can make up for time lost? Swazi “We are worried but its education versus life of people you know even the president needs to make that decision because you can’t say lets go back to school because we are worried when we known that Covid 19 is real.” Sphe “I am worried when I go back to school there will be too many of us in one classroom.” Basil “We know that at or schools in their present make up social distancing is almost impossible, but what I want to reassure people about is that no teacher union is going to sit back and certainly not NAAPTOSA and just say for the gettinb the year sarted lets just go back , no parent is going to do that and we are dealing with concerns about teachers saying you know I am 64, we are dealing with prents who are saying I am so terrified can I keep my child at home, these are real concerns. How many of our teachers in our schools are immune defficient. This is what we have put on the table with the DBE, with this I want to show how much thinking is going into this.” V/O There are no definite answers, we will have to see how the pandemic progresses but in the interim there many futures at stake. Asanda “When we were kids I usually spoke a lot about being a scientistst but then life has its ways you don’t always get what you want.” Ntando “And so it hurts to know that we grew up as children with the same aspirations to finish school go work, help out our families but there is a possibility that only one person out of the three will realise their dreams and it is heart breaking.” Promo 1 Its affected 1.5 billion learners from 191 countries around the world, how is the COVID 19 pandemic lockdown affecting children’s education in South Africa. Promo 2 Experts have said that we have lost to much time due to the Covid 19 lockdown and should just scrap the 2020 educational year. Should we just pass all the children or can we still salvage their education? Promo 3 The Department of Basic Education is confident that the 2020 SCHOOL year is not lost (and they have a comphrehensive recovery plan.) But can the 10 million learners who are not receiving tuition at the moment catch up?

metadata.Further information: There has been so much uncertainty to deal with during our lockdown; infection rates are soaring , economies are crumbling and unemployement is rife. There is a great sense of anxiety with the uncertainty. Professor Jonathan Jansen’s SABC interview where he suggested that we should just scrap the 2020 academic year has really upset the apple cart amongst educationalists and parents. https://citizen.co.za/parenty/2270703/watch-prof-jansen-says-scrap-entire-2020-school-year-pass-all-students/ https://mybroadband.co.za/news/government/347959-scrap-school-year-and-pass-all-learners-professor-jansen.html The Department of Education has said that his comments were irresponsible and premature. Elijah Mhlanga, the spokesperson states that after lockdown the learners will only have missed half of a term. And that the Department of Education is working on a plan. https://www.msn.com/en-za/news/other/dbe-dismisses-call-to-scrap-school-year-as-irresponsible/ar-BB12M1r1 There is no plan as yet. Understandably we haven’t seen the full force of Covid in our country yet. All schools were closed on the 18th of March 2020. Minister Angie Motshekga said at the time that “we have determined that schools should resume on 14 April 2020; unless determined differently. If that happens,we will communicate with parents. We are going to lose 10 school days as a result of the school closures. To compensate for lost days, the June holidays will be cut short by a week. Once opened, schools will be encouraged to extend tuition hours.” It was anticipated that pupils would return to school on the 14th of April, until Pres Ramaphosa extended lockdown for another two weeks. He has also suggested that there may be a phased return for the citizens of South Africa. What is the plan now and what does that mean for the learners of the country? There is a pressure to get our economy back to work but the threat of Covid may not have passed. While there is uncertainty, can we really afford to scrap a year as Jonathan Jansen suggests. Carte Blanche sets out to see what the impact of the lockdown has been on education and what solutions there may be. We have identified 4 schools to speak to in KZN, a private school, a rural school, a model C school and a township school. We have an academic at UKZN and have asked for an interview with the spokesperson of the Department of Education. The questions that have been raised due to the Covid lockdown are; - Are all the schools teaching at the moment? - Private schools and model C schools seem to be teaching again on learning platforms. But what about the State Schools? - What support has been given to schools? - Can we make up the time that has been lost? - Can our teachers cope with the new way of teaching via e learning and other platforms? - When will it be safe to send the kids back to school? - Its not just their education at stake but their health? - How can we assure the protection of the pupils at schools where there is no running water and sanitation? - Can we afford to have the class sizes that we had in the past – what about social distancing? - What about fees? Should parents continue to pay if they are not receiving the teaching that they were promised and the childrena re staying at home? - Will the divide between the haves and have nots just be increased at this time? Private schools have resources to technology and poorer schools don’t even have accessibility to data. - Some of the children have also been negatively affected because they have not had access to te daily meal that the school provides. - Parents are hungry and unemployed getting food is more important than education. - There are solutions that have been suggested. Working on Saturdays, reducing the work load for the year. Shortening the holidays. - Unusual times calls for unusual measures. - Dr Imran Keeka says that 80% of our learners do not have the necessary facilities. - There will be a huge amount of infrastructure to mobilise to get this working. Jojo Tanks and toilets. Connectivity. - How will we cope if there is a 2nd and 3rd wave of COVID 19? - And what about the psychological implication. Children will be unsettled. They will have experienced a great change in the world. Close ones may have died. How will they cope going back to school? Is there the necessary psychological support? - Matrics? Agreed to be interviewed. 1. Principal Swazi Shabangu - Susan Ngcobo Amaoti Inanda 0838253534 Nothing happening. No direction from department. Not teaching. Trying to reach out to parents way forward academic year. Parents aren’t working and more worried about food. At school they used to provide free lunch.NGO provide food parcels. They used to cook at school. Tried to get approval to feed at school but denied. 2.Clifton School Private Boys. All teachers teaching on microsoft teams. Mr Shaun McCabe 0848500860 will talk to us. Everything back to normal. Boys having lessons with teachers on line. They do sometimes struggle with connectivity. But with resources all going well. 3. Dr Sihle Memela. Principal of High Flats. Rural School. 120km away from Durban. 082 7648618 No education doesn’t know what is happening. Sending some info on whatsapp. Some people doing it and some people not. Not sure if they will go back to teaching as they may not be getting raise in July. Talk of turning school in boarding school. Want all kids and teachers to be tested for Covid before they go back. 4. Prof Labby Ramrathan UKZN School of Education Studies 0826749829 15 Edgcot Rd Westville Can make time up. Teach them not all content but skills they need to master. Can work holidays and can work saturdays. Not the end of the school year. Curriculum not so extensive.Doesnt agree with Jansen. What is possible Focus on elements competance progress into next grade Essential elements of next grade Subject specialist overall perspecive of curriculum What element current curriculum Distilled version of year. Most knowledge is worthwhile right now. Content manage next year Learner manager platforms Poor infrastructure Provide community members help Can’t have 60 – 80 in class room Open up spaces. Extend school hours Opportunity avaliable Reduce holidays difficult 1 week holiday, reduce, can also utilise Saturdays 5. American software, for free during COVID for next two moths. 90% of kids are able to connect. Can connect on phone. 6.
